decks.title: Principles of Management — Part 1: Nature, Significance and Fayol
goals: Explain the meaning and the nature of principles of management
Explain why principles of management are significant
Explain Fayol's fourteen principles and identify them in business situations
Distinguish between unity of command and unity of direction

slides.heading: Principles of Management
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what principles are, their **nature** and **significance**, and **Fayol's fourteen principles**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: what principles of management are, their nature, why they matter, Fayol's fourteen principles, and applying them to cases
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Welcome. Every manager, whether she runs a school canteen or a steel plant, faces the same questions. Who should report to whom? How should work be divided? How do we treat people fairly? Over the years, managers have collected answers to such questions as general rules called principles of management. In this part we see what they are, why they matter, and the fourteen principles given by Henri Fayol.

slides.heading: What is a principle of management?
slides.body_md: A **principle of management** is a broad, general **guideline** for decision-making and behaviour. It is not a technique and not a value.

rows: A broad, general guideline for decisions and behaviour
A procedure or method used to do a task
Unity of command: one boss for each employee
Time study: fixing the standard time of a job
Guides the choice and use of techniques

visual.alt: Table comparing a principle and a technique of management: a principle is a broad guideline such as unity of command; a technique is a method such as time study; principles guide how techniques are chosen and used

slides.narration: A principle of management is a broad and general guideline for making decisions and for behaviour at work. Do not confuse it with a technique. A technique is a method for doing a task, such as time study. A principle is wider: it guides how we choose and use techniques. For example, unity of command tells us that each employee should have one boss.

slides.heading: Nature of principles

rows: Applies to every kind of organisation
A temple trust and a car maker both divide work
Grew from managers' experience and tests
A bakery learns from trial batches
Strict rules in a big plant, looser in a small one
Team spirit in a call centre
Fair pay leads to lower turnover
More delegation as a firm grows

visual.alt: Table of the seven features of the nature of principles of management: universal applicability, general guidelines, formed by practice and experimentation, flexible, mainly behavioural, cause and effect, and contingent, each with its meaning and an imagined example

slides.narration: Principles of management have seven features. They apply to all organisations. They are general guidelines, not ready-made answers. They were formed by practice and experiments. They are flexible and are mainly about human behaviour. They show a cause and effect link between action and result. And they are contingent, which means their use depends on the situation. Learn each feature with a short example.

slides.heading: Quick check: which feature?
slides.body_md: A hospital, a software firm and a cricket academy all use the same principles. Which feature is this?
slides.narration: Here is a quick check. Ask yourself whether the example is about where principles apply, how they work, or when they work.

slides.heading: Significance of principles

nodes.label: Optimum use of resources and effective administration

visual.alt: Flow listing six reasons why principles of management matter: insights into reality, optimum use of resources and effective administration, scientific decisions, meeting a changing environment, fulfilling social responsibility, and management training, education and research
visual.caption: Why principles matter

slides.narration: Why should managers study principles? First, they give useful insights into reality, so a manager can foresee problems. Second, they help use resources well and make administration impersonal and fair. Third, they lead to scientific decisions based on reasoning. Fourth, they help firms adjust to change. Fifth, they guide social responsibility, such as fair wages. Sixth, they are the base of management training and research.

slides.heading: Fayol and his fourteen principles
slides.body_md: Henri Fayol, a French mining engineer and manager, wrote about general management from the point of view of **top management**. His principles came from his **personal experience**.
bullets: Known as the **father of general management**.
Gave **fourteen** principles that apply to all organisations.

rows: Split work into small tasks; specialisation raises efficiency
Obey rules and agreements; both sides keep them
One head, one plan for activities with one objective
Fair pay within the firm's capacity

visual.alt: Table of Fayol's principles one to seven: division of work, authority and responsibility, discipline, unity of command, unity of direction, subordination of individual interest to general interest, and remuneration of employees, each summarised in one line
visual.caption: Fayol's principles (1–7)

slides.narration: Henri Fayol was a French engineer who rose to head a large mining company. He studied management from the top, using his own long experience, and he is called the father of general management. He gave fourteen principles. This table shows the first seven: division of work, authority and responsibility, discipline, unity of command, unity of direction, subordination of individual interest, and fair remuneration.

slides.heading: Fayol's principles 8 to 14

rows: Find the right balance for the firm
Formal line of authority, top to bottom; gang plank in emergencies
A place for everything and everyone, and each in its place
Do not move or remove employees too often
Encourage employees to suggest and carry out improvements

visual.alt: Table of Fayol's principles eight to fourteen: centralisation and decentralisation, scalar chain, order, equity, stability of tenure of personnel, initiative, and esprit de corps, each summarised in one line
visual.caption: Fayol's principles (8–14)

slides.narration: Here are the other seven. Centralisation and decentralisation need a balance. The scalar chain is the formal line of authority. Order means a place for everything and everyone. Equity means fairness without discrimination. Stability of tenure means employees should not be moved too often. Initiative means encouraging suggestions. And esprit de corps means team spirit.

slides.heading: Unity of command
slides.body_md: Each employee should receive orders from **one superior only**.
bullets: Two bosses → **dual subordination**: confusion, conflict, weak discipline.
Example: a carpenter told by two supervisors to do opposite things.

nodes.label: Two bosses give orders to one worker

visual.alt: Flow showing what happens when unity of command is violated: two bosses give conflicting orders, the worker is confused, and discipline and output suffer
visual.caption: When unity of command is broken

slides.narration: Unity of command says that every employee should take orders from only one boss. When two bosses give orders, the worker does not know whom to obey, especially if the orders conflict. This is called dual subordination. It causes confusion, weakens discipline and lowers output. In case questions, look for one person getting instructions from two people.

slides.heading: Quick check: two supervisors
slides.body_md: A carpenter is given conflicting orders by two supervisors. Which principle is violated?
slides.narration: Try this one. Count how many people are giving orders to the carpenter.

slides.heading: Unity of command vs unity of direction
columns:
**Unity of command**

One boss for each **employee**.

**Unity of direction**

One head and one plan for each **group of activities** with the same objective.

rows: One head and one plan for a group of activities with one objective
The organisation or a division as a whole

visual.alt: Table distinguishing unity of command from unity of direction: the first means one boss for each employee, aims to prevent dual subordination and concerns the individual; the second means one head and one plan for activities with one objective, aims at coordination and concerns the organisation

slides.narration: Students often mix up these two. Unity of command is about one employee and one boss. Unity of direction is about a group of activities with the same objective, which should have one head and one plan. The first prevents dual subordination. The second prevents overlapping work and helps coordination. One concerns the individual, the other the organisation.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: one firm, two principles
slides.body_md: An imagined snack maker in Patna has separate heads and plans for namkeen and sweets, but one packer takes orders from both heads.
bullets: Step 1 — Separate heads and plans for each product line: **unity of direction followed**.
Step 2 — One packer, two heads: **unity of command violated**.
Step 3 — Fix: each packer reports to one head only.

rows: Namkeen and sweets have separate heads and plans
A packer gets orders from both heads

visual.alt: Worked example table for an imagined snack maker in Patna: separate heads and plans for namkeen and sweets follow unity of direction, but a packer taking orders from both heads violates unity of command
visual.caption: One firm can follow one principle and break the other

slides.narration: Let us apply the difference. The snack maker has one head and one plan for namkeen and another for sweets, so unity of direction is followed. But one packer takes orders from both heads, so unity of command is violated. A firm can follow one principle and break the other at the same time. The fix is simple: each packer reports to only one head.

slides.narration: The scalar chain is the formal line of authority from the top to the bottom. Normally, if D wants to talk to H, the message goes up to A and comes down the other side. That is slow. In an emergency, Fayol allowed a gang plank, a direct link between D and H at the same level, provided both inform their superiors. The chain is still respected.

slides.heading: Quick check: the place for everything
slides.body_md: Every bin is labelled and every worker has a fixed workstation. Which principle is this?
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about which principle is about places for things and people.

slides.heading: Fair treatment: equity, remuneration, discipline
bullets: **Equity:** kindliness and justice; no discrimination on religion, caste, gender, language or region.
**Remuneration:** fair pay, a reasonable standard of living, within the firm's capacity.
**Discipline:** obedience to rules and agreements, needing good superiors, clear agreements and fair penalties.

rows: Pay is far below the area

visual.alt: Table of three fairness principles and how they are violated: equity when promotions go only to relatives, remuneration when pay is far below the area, discipline when management breaks the wage agreement

slides.narration: Three principles are about fair treatment. Equity means kindness and justice, with no discrimination. Remuneration means pay that is fair to workers and that the firm can afford. Discipline means both sides obey rules and agreements. Notice that discipline is not only for workers: if management breaks its own promises, discipline breaks down too.

slides.heading: People and team: stability, initiative, esprit de corps
bullets: **Stability of tenure:** do not move or remove staff too often; they need time to learn.
**Initiative:** encourage suggestions, for example through a suggestion box with rewards.
**Esprit de corps:** build team spirit; say **we**, not **I**.

visual.alt: Flow showing that stable jobs, freedom to suggest and team spirit together lead to committed and productive employees
visual.caption: Principles that build commitment

slides.narration: The last group of principles builds commitment. Stability of tenure means people are not moved or removed too often, because they need time to learn the job. Initiative means encouraging employees to suggest and carry out improvements. Esprit de corps means team spirit. A manager who says we instead of I, and shares credit, builds it.

slides.heading: How to answer a case question

nodes.label: Read the case; underline key lines
Match each line to one principle
Quote the line and explain in one sentence

visual.alt: Flow of the method for case questions: read the case and underline key lines, match each line to one principle, name the principle exactly, then quote the line and explain it in one sentence
visual.caption: How to answer a case question

slides.narration: Board papers love short cases. Use a four step method. Read the case and underline the key lines. Match each line to exactly one principle. Write the name of the principle in full. Then quote the line from the case and explain it in one sentence. Marks are given for the correct name and for the link to the case.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: spotting principles in a case
slides.body_md: An imagined printing press in Indore. Identify the principle in each line.
bullets: Step 1 — Underline: one in-charge; marked racks; bonus for suggestions; the Press Family.
Step 2 — Match each line to a principle.
Step 3 — Quote and explain.

headers: Line in the case (imagined Indore printing press)
rows: Each press operator reports only to the floor in-charge
Paper rolls are stacked in marked racks
Operators who suggest faster changeovers get a bonus
The owner calls the team "the Press Family" at every meeting

visual.alt: Worked example table for an imagined printing press in Indore: reporting to one in-charge shows unity of command, marked racks show order, bonuses for suggestions show initiative, and calling the team a family shows esprit de corps
visual.caption: Worked example: identifying principles from case lines

slides.narration: Let us practise the method on an imagined printing press. Operators report only to the floor in charge: unity of command. Paper rolls are stacked in marked racks: order. Operators who suggest faster changeovers get a bonus: initiative. The owner calls the team the press family: esprit de corps. Notice how each line points to one principle only.

slides.heading: Quick check: true or false?
slides.body_md: Under the gang plank, the two employees' superiors must be kept informed. True or false?
slides.narration: One more check. Remember why Fayol allowed the gang plank, and what he did not want to lose.

slides.heading: Summary

rows: Universal, guidelines, practice, flexible, behavioural, cause and effect, contingent
Insights, resources, scientific decisions, change, social responsibility, training
Division, authority, discipline, command, direction, subordination, remuneration, centralisation, scalar chain, order, equity, stability, initiative, esprit de corps

visual.alt: Summary table: seven features of principles, six reasons for their significance, and the key words for Fayol's fourteen principles

slides.narration: To sum up. A principle is a broad guideline. Principles have seven features and six kinds of significance. Fayol gave fourteen principles from the point of view of top management. Remember the difference between unity of command and unity of direction, and the gang plank as an emergency short cut in the scalar chain.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write the **full name** of the principle: "subordination of individual interest to general interest", not just "subordination".
In cases, **quote the line** and then explain; one principle per line.
Equity is **fairness**, not equal pay.
Discipline binds **both** management and workers.
For differences, use **bases** (meaning, aim, concerns) and write both sides for each.

rows: Name of the principle or feature
Three points, or principle + line + explanation
Five points or five bases, each explained

visual.alt: Table of how marks are awarded: one mark for the name, three marks for three points or a principle with quoted line and explanation, five marks for five explained points or bases

slides.narration: Some exam tips. Always write the full name of a principle. In case questions, quote the line and explain, one principle per line. Remember that equity means fairness, not equal pay, and that discipline binds management too. For differences, choose clear bases and write both sides for each one.

decks.title: Principles of Management — Part 2: Taylor's Scientific Management
goals: Explain Taylor's four principles of scientific management
Explain the techniques of scientific management, including functional foremanship
Calculate earnings under the differential piece wage system
Compare the contributions of Fayol and Taylor

slides.heading: Scientific management
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **F. W. Taylor**, the four **principles** and the **techniques** of scientific management.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: Taylor and scientific management, its four principles, its techniques, the differential piece wage system, and a comparison of Fayol and Taylor
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Frederick Winslow Taylor was an American engineer who worked his way up on the shop floor. He asked a simple question: is there one best way to do each job? His answer, built from careful observation and experiments, is called scientific management. We will study his four principles, his techniques and a simple wage calculation.

slides.heading: What is scientific management?
slides.body_md: Knowing exactly what you want people to do, and seeing that they do it in the **best and cheapest** way.
bullets: Taylor is called the **father of scientific management**.
Based on **observation and experiments** at the shop floor.

nodes.label: Old way: rule of thumb, habit and guesswork

visual.alt: Flow from the old way of rule of thumb and guesswork, through scientific study of the job, to one best way and higher output at lower cost
visual.caption: From rule of thumb to science

slides.narration: Scientific management means deciding exactly what each worker should do, and seeing that it is done in the best and cheapest way. Before Taylor, most factories ran on rule of thumb, that is, habit and guesswork. Taylor replaced guesswork with study and experiment, so that every job had one best method.

slides.heading: The four principles

rows: Study each job to find the one best way
End conflict through a mental revolution; share gains
Managers and workers work together; workers' suggestions welcomed
Development of each and every person
Scientific selection, placement and training for greatest efficiency

visual.alt: Table of Taylor's four principles: science not rule of thumb, harmony not discord, cooperation not individualism, and development of each and every person to greatest efficiency and prosperity

slides.narration: Taylor gave four principles. Science, not rule of thumb: study each job to find the best way. Harmony, not discord: management and workers should stop fighting. Cooperation, not individualism: they should work together and share ideas. And development of each and every person: select, place and train every worker scientifically to reach the greatest efficiency.

slides.heading: Harmony and the mental revolution

nodes.label: Old attitude: fight over the share of surplus

visual.alt: Flow of the mental revolution: from fighting over the share of the surplus, both sides change attitude, raise the surplus together and enjoy higher wages and profits
visual.caption: Harmony, not discord

slides.narration: Taylor believed that managers and workers often fought over how to divide the surplus. He called for a mental revolution, a complete change of attitude on both sides. Instead of fighting over the size of each share, they should work together to make the surplus bigger. Then both wages and profits can rise.

slides.heading: Quick check: name the technique
slides.body_md: A consultant films stitchers and removes three needless hand movements. Which technique is this?
slides.narration: Quick check. Is the consultant fixing time, fixing rest, or removing movements?

visual.caption: Eight specialist foremen: four plan, four supervise production.

slides.narration: Taylor felt that one foreman could not be expert in everything. So he separated planning from doing and gave each worker eight specialist foremen. Four work under the planning in charge: the route clerk, instruction card clerk, time and cost clerk, and disciplinarian. Four work under the production in charge: the speed boss, gang boss, repair boss and inspector.

slides.heading: Who does what?

rows: Sees that rules and regulations are followed
Sees that work is done on time and at the right speed
Keeps machines, tools and materials ready

visual.alt: Table of the eight specialist foremen and their jobs: route clerk, instruction card clerk, time and cost clerk, disciplinarian, speed boss, gang boss, repair boss and inspector

slides.narration: Here are the jobs. The route clerk fixes the sequence of work. The instruction card clerk writes the instructions. The time and cost clerk prepares time and cost sheets. sections.heading: 1. Meaning and nature of principles of management
sections.body_md:
A **principle of management** is a broad, general guideline for decision-making and behaviour. It differs from a **technique** (a method for doing a task) and from a **value** (a moral belief).

**Nature (seven features):**
1. **Universal applicability:** all organisations, business and non-business, large and small.
2. **General guidelines:** not ready-made solutions; applied with judgement.
3. **Formed by practice and experimentation.**
4. **Flexible:** adapted to the situation.
5. **Mainly behavioural:** aim to influence how people behave.
6. **Cause and effect relationship:** link actions to likely results.
7. **Contingent:** their use depends on the situation.

key_terms.definition_md: A broad, general guideline for decisions and behaviour of managers.
Depending on the situation in which a principle is applied.

rows: Applies to every kind of organisation
A temple trust and a car maker both divide work
Grew from managers' experience and tests
A bakery learns from trial batches
Strict rules in a big plant, looser in a small one
Team spirit in a call centre
Fair pay leads to lower turnover
More delegation as a firm grows

sections.heading: 2. Significance of principles of management
sections.body_md:
1. **Useful insights into reality:** managers understand situations better and foresee problems.
2. **Optimum use of resources and effective administration:** less trial and error; impersonal, fair administration.
3. **Scientific decisions:** based on objective reasoning, not bias.
4. **Meeting a changing environment:** flexible principles help firms adapt to new technology and competition.
5. **Fulfilling social responsibility:** for example, fair pay and fair treatment.
6. **Management training, education and research:** principles are the base of management studies.

key_terms.definition_md: Decisions based on rules and reasoning rather than personal likes and dislikes.

sections.heading: 3. Fayol's principles of management
sections.body_md:
Henri Fayol (French mining engineer and manager; **father of general management**) gave fourteen principles from the point of view of **top management**, based on his **experience**.

1. **Division of work** — specialisation. 2. **Authority and responsibility** — balance. 3. **Discipline** — obedience to rules and agreements by both sides; needs good superiors, clear agreements, judicious penalties. 4. **Unity of command** — one boss per employee. 5. **Unity of direction** — one head, one plan for activities with one objective. 6. **Subordination of individual interest to general interest.** 7. **Remuneration of employees** — fair, within paying capacity. 8. **Centralisation and decentralisation** — balance. 9. **Scalar chain** — formal line of authority; **gang plank** for emergencies, superiors informed. 10. **Order** — a place for everything and everyone. 11. **Equity** — kindliness and justice, no discrimination. 12. **Stability of tenure of personnel.** 13. **Initiative** — suggestions encouraged. 14. **Esprit de corps** — team spirit.

A direct link between two employees at the same level for quick communication in an emergency.
Team spirit and unity among employees.

sections.heading: 5. Taylor's principles of scientific management
sections.body_md:
F. W. Taylor (American engineer; **father of scientific management**) worked through **observation and experiments** on the shop floor.

1. **Science, not rule of thumb:** study each job to find the one best way.
2. **Harmony, not discord:** end class conflict through a **mental revolution**; both sides share the gains.
3. **Cooperation, not individualism:** management welcomes workers' suggestions; workers do not strike without reason.
4. **Development of each and every person to his or her greatest efficiency and prosperity:** scientific selection, placement and training.

key_terms.definition_md: Deciding by habit, guesswork or personal judgement instead of study.
A change of attitude by management and workers from conflict to cooperation.

Scientific selection, placement and training for greatest efficiency

sections.heading: 6. Techniques of scientific management
sections.body_md:
1. **Functional foremanship:** planning separated from execution; eight specialists. **Planning in-charge:** route clerk, instruction card clerk, time and cost clerk, disciplinarian. **Production in-charge:** speed boss, gang boss, repair boss, inspector.
2. **Standardisation and simplification of work:** fixed standards; removal of unnecessary varieties.
3. **Method study:** the one best way of doing the job.
4. **Motion study:** eliminating needless movements.
5. **Time study:** standard time for a well-defined job.
6. **Fatigue study:** frequency and length of rest intervals.
7. **Differential piece wage system:** a higher rate per piece at or above the standard output, a lower rate below it.

sections.heading: 7. Fayol and Taylor compared
sections.body_md: Perspective: top management (Fayol) vs shop floor (Taylor). Unity of command: followed (Fayol) vs violated by functional foremanship (Taylor). Applicability: universal vs specialised situations. Basis: personal experience vs observation and experiments. Focus: overall administration vs productivity. Their contributions **complement** each other.

visual.alt: Table comparing Fayol and Taylor: Fayol took a top-management view, followed unity of command, gave universal principles from experience and focused on administration; Taylor worked from the shop floor, broke unity of command, gave principles for specialised situations from experiments and focused on productivity

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing a short name ("subordination") instead of the full name of a principle.
- Confusing **unity of command** (one boss) with **unity of direction** (one head, one plan).
- Saying equity means equal pay.
- Mixing up motion study and time study, or standardisation and simplification.
- Placing the eight foremen under the wrong in-charge.
- In wage sums, applying the higher rate below the standard.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: the name of the principle, feature or technique.
- 3 marks: three explained points, or principle + quoted line + explanation.
- 4 marks (case): each part asks for an identification and an explanation from the case.
- 5 marks: five points or five bases, each explained.

**Cases in SOYL practice** are imagined; your board paper will give its own situation. Always quote the line you rely on.

cards.back_md: A broad, general **guideline** for decisions and behaviour.
Principle: a guideline (unity of command). Technique: a method (time study).
Universal, general guidelines, practice and experimentation, flexible, behavioural, cause and effect, contingent.
The use of a principle **depends on the situation**.
Insights; resources and administration; scientific decisions; change; social responsibility; training and research.

cards.front_md: Who is the father of **general management**?
cards.back_md: **Henri Fayol**.
Each employee gets orders from **one** superior only.
**One head and one plan** for a group of activities with the same objective.
One employee, two bosses: violates unity of command.
The formal line of authority from the highest to the lowest rank.
Direct contact between same-level employees in an **emergency**, superiors informed.
A place for everything and everyone, and everything and everyone in its place.
Kindliness and justice; **no discrimination**. Not equal pay.
Good superiors, clear and fair agreements, judicious penalties.
Fair pay: a reasonable standard of living, within the firm's capacity.
Do not move or remove employees too often.
Encourage employees to suggest and carry out improvements.
Team spirit: we, not I.

cards.front_md: Purchase from a relative at a higher price: which principle is broken?
cards.back_md: **Subordination of individual interest to general interest**.

cards.front_md: Who is the father of **scientific management**?
cards.back_md: **F. W. Taylor**.
Science, not rule of thumb; harmony, not discord; cooperation, not individualism; development of each person.
Management and workers change from conflict to cooperation and share gains.
Route clerk, instruction card clerk, time and cost clerk, disciplinarian.
Speed boss, gang boss, repair boss, inspector.
Motion: remove needless movements. Time: fix the standard time.
Fixes the amount and frequency of rest intervals.
Finds the one best way of doing the whole job.
Removing unnecessary varieties, sizes and grades of a product.
Higher rate per piece at or above the standard; lower rate below it.

cards.front_md: Which technique violates unity of command?
cards.back_md: **Functional foremanship** (eight bosses).

cards.front_md: Fayol vs Taylor: perspective and basis
cards.back_md: Fayol: top management, experience. Taylor: shop floor, experiments.

questions.stem_md: The principles of management can be used by a hospital in Kochi, a software firm in Pune and a cricket academy in Ranchi alike. Which feature of principles does this show?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Universal applicability. Principles apply to every kind of organisation, large or small, business or non-business, which is universal applicability. The other options are features too, but they describe what principles deal with (behaviour), how they work (cause and effect) or when they apply (contingent).

questions.stem_md: Meher, owner of an imagined bakery chain in Indore, divides work strictly in her large central kitchen but lets the three staff in a small outlet share all tasks. Which feature of principles of management does her approach show?

options.text_md: Flexible: they can be adapted to the situation

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Flexible: they can be adapted to the situation. She applies the same principle (division of work) differently in a big and a small unit. Principles are flexible and are modified to suit the situation. "General guidelines that never change" is wrong: principles are general guidelines but they do change and are adapted.

questions.stem_md: Why are principles of management described as **mainly behavioural**?

options.text_md: They aim to influence the behaviour of people working in the organisation
They are derived from laboratory experiments on machines
They give exact results, like the laws of physics
They apply only to the behaviour of customers

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** They aim to influence the behaviour of people working in the organisation. Management works through people, so its principles guide human behaviour and relationships at work. They are not exact like physical laws, and they concern employees, not only customers.

questions.stem_md: Principles of management are called **general guidelines** because

options.text_md: they are rules that must be followed word for word in every case
they are laws passed by Parliament for companies
they are not ready-made solutions; their use depends on the situation
they cover only general administration and not production

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** they are not ready-made solutions; their use depends on the situation. Principles guide action but do not give fixed answers; real situations are complex, so the manager has to judge how to apply them. They are not rigid rules or legal provisions.

questions.stem_md: A manager at an imagined courier firm in Guwahati finds that strict centralisation worked when the firm had two branches but slows decisions now that it has forty. The feature of principles that explains this is that they are

options.text_md: contingent: their use depends on the prevailing situation

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** contingent: their use depends on the prevailing situation. The usefulness of a principle depends on the conditions in which it is applied; as the firm grows, the right degree of centralisation changes. That is the contingent nature of principles.

questions.stem_md: Principles of management have been developed mainly

options.text_md: through the practice, observation and experiments of managers
by courts while deciding business disputes

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** through the practice, observation and experiments of managers. Principles are formed by practice and experimentation: managers observed what worked, tested it and generalised it into guidelines.

questions.stem_md: A newly promoted manager at an imagined textile mill in Surat reads about principles of management and now foresees which of her decisions could cause conflict. Which significance of principles does this illustrate?

options.text_md: Meeting the requirements of a changing environment
Providing managers with useful insights into reality

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Providing managers with useful insights into reality. Understanding principles improves a manager's knowledge and foresight, so she can anticipate problems: this is the significance of giving useful insights into reality.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Principles of management help managers predict the likely result of a decision.

**Reason (R):** Principles establish a cause and effect relationship between actions and their results.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: because a principle links an action to its likely result, a manager can predict what will happen if it is applied.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Principles of management are as exact as the principles of pure science.

**Reason (R):** Principles of management deal with human behaviour, which cannot be predicted with full accuracy.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: management principles are not exact, since they deal with people. R is true, and it is the very reason A is false.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Principles of management help a business fulfil its social responsibility, for example by guiding fair wages for employees.
questions.solution_md: **True.** Principles such as fair remuneration and equity guide managers towards fair treatment of employees and the wider society, which is part of social responsibility.

questions.stem_md: Principles of management apply to all kinds of organisations, business as well as non-business. This feature is called ___ applicability.
questions.solution_md: This is the universal applicability of principles.

questions.stem_md: Explain any two features of the nature of principles of management.
questions.solution_md: Two features, each named and explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Flexible:** principles are not rigid; a manager adapts them to the **needs of the situation**.
2. **Mainly behavioural:** they aim to influence the **behaviour of people** at work, since management gets work done through others.

questions.stem_md: How do principles of management help in the optimum use of resources and in effective administration?
questions.solution_md: One point on resources and one on administration.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Resources:** principles help managers foresee the **cause and effect** of decisions, so men, money and materials are not wasted on trial and error.
**Administration:** they make management **impersonal**, limiting personal bias, so decisions are fair and consistent.

questions.stem_md: The manager of an imagined chain of pharmacies in Lucknow says that principles of management are only common sense and are not worth studying. Give three reasons to show that he is mistaken.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct points of significance, each linked to why study is useful.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Scientific decisions:** principles make decisions **objective** and based on reasoning, not on personal bias or guesswork.
2. **Meeting change:** principles are flexible, so they help managers adapt to **changes in technology and competition**, for example when moving to online orders.
3. **Training and research:** principles are the **basis of management education** and help train new managers quickly.

questions.stem_md: Explain any five features that describe the nature of principles of management.
questions.solution_md: Any five features, each named and briefly explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Universal applicability:** they apply to every organisation, business or non-business, large or small.
2. **General guidelines:** they guide action but are not ready-made solutions for every problem.
3. **Formed by practice and experimentation:** they grew out of managers' experience and experiments.
4. **Flexible:** managers modify them to suit the situation.
5. **Cause and effect relationship:** they link an action to its likely result, so outcomes can be predicted. (Also: mainly behavioural; contingent.)

questions.stem_md: At an imagined furniture factory in Jodhpur, a carpenter receives orders from both the production supervisor and the quality supervisor, and the orders conflict. Which principle of Fayol is violated?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Unity of command. Unity of command says each employee should receive orders from **one** superior only. Two bosses giving conflicting orders is dual subordination. Unity of direction is about one plan and one head for a group of activities with the same objective.

questions.stem_md: An imagined company in Chennai makes both air coolers and water purifiers. It sets up two separate divisions, each with its own head, plan and staff. Which principle is being followed?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Unity of direction. One head and one plan for each group of activities with the same objective is unity of direction. Unity of command concerns how many bosses one employee has.

questions.stem_md: According to Fayol, the **scalar chain** refers to

options.text_md: the equal treatment of all employees
the formal line of authority from the highest to the lowest rank
the arrangement of materials in their proper places
the division of a job into small tasks

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** the formal line of authority from the highest to the lowest rank. The scalar chain is the formal line of authority that communications follow from top to bottom. Equal treatment is equity, proper places is order, and small tasks is division of work.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined steel plant in Bhilai, a furnace supervisor needs coolant urgently from a stores supervisor at the same level. The usual route goes up three levels and down three. What did Fayol suggest for such an emergency?

options.text_md: Wait for the message to travel along the full scalar chain
Ask the managing director to decide personally
A gang plank: direct contact between the two, with their superiors informed
Transfer one supervisor to the other department

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A gang plank: direct contact between the two, with their superiors informed. Fayol allowed a gang plank so that employees at the same level can communicate directly in an emergency, keeping their superiors informed. Waiting for the full chain would cause delay.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined auto-parts warehouse in Gurugram, every bin is labelled and every worker has a fixed workstation, so nothing is wasted searching. Which principle does this follow?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Order. Order means a place for everything and everyone, and everything and everyone in its place. Discipline concerns obedience to rules; equity is fairness; initiative is about suggestions for improvement.

questions.stem_md: The HR head of an imagined hotel in Jaipur insists that promotions be decided on performance alone, whatever the employee's religion, gender or home state. Which principle is applied?

options.text_md: Subordination of individual interest to general interest

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Equity. Equity calls for kindliness and justice, with no discrimination on grounds such as religion, gender or region.

questions.stem_md: The team leader at an imagined call centre in Mohali always says "we achieved the target" and holds weekly team lunches. Which principle is she promoting?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Esprit de corps. Esprit de corps means team spirit and unity; replacing "I" with "we" builds it.

questions.stem_md: An imagined biscuit company in Kolkata pays a bonus to any worker whose suggestion cuts wastage on the packing line. Which principle of Fayol is this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Initiative. Encouraging employees to think of and carry out improvements, for example through a suggestion scheme, is the principle of initiative.

questions.stem_md: An imagined bank in Bhopal transfers its loan officers to a new branch every three months. Customers complain that officers never learn the local business. Which principle is being ignored?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Stability of tenure of personnel. Employees should not be moved too often; they need time to learn the job and become effective. Frequent transfers violate stability of tenure.

questions.stem_md: A purchase manager at an imagined cement company in Raipur wants to buy from his cousin's firm at a higher price. The director refuses and buys from the cheapest reliable supplier. Which principle does the director uphold?

options.text_md: Subordination of individual interest to general interest

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Subordination of individual interest to general interest. The interest of the organisation must come before the interest of any individual; the manager's family interest cannot override the company's.

questions.stem_md: Fayol's principle of authority and responsibility states that

options.text_md: a manager should have authority but no responsibility
all authority should remain with the top manager
responsibility can be delegated completely to subordinates
there should be a balance (parity) between the authority given and the responsibility placed on a person

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** there should be a balance (parity) between the authority given and the responsibility placed on a person. Authority without responsibility can be misused, and responsibility without authority makes work impossible, so the two must be balanced.

questions.stem_md: Under Fayol's principle of **remuneration of employees**, wages should be

options.text_md: fair to employees and within the paying capacity of the firm
as low as possible to maximise profit
the same for every employee whatever the job
decided only by the workers' union

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** fair to employees and within the paying capacity of the firm. Pay should give employees at least a reasonable standard of living and be within what the company can afford, so both sides gain.

questions.stem_md: An imagined garment exporter in Tiruppur agreed to pay overtime at double rate but stopped doing so; workers then stopped following the shift rules. Which principle did the management break first?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Discipline. Discipline means obedience to organisational rules and the employment agreement **by both sides**; it needs fair agreements kept by management. The firm broke the agreement first.

questions.stem_md: Division of work leads to

options.text_md: a breakdown in the line of authority
specialisation, which increases speed, accuracy and efficiency

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** specialisation, which increases speed, accuracy and efficiency. Dividing a job into small tasks lets each worker specialise and become more efficient.

questions.stem_md: The owner of an imagined chain of 25 restaurants in Hyderabad decides menus and prices herself but lets each outlet manager hire staff and order supplies. Which principle explains this balance?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Centralisation and decentralisation. Fayol said no organisation is fully centralised or fully decentralised; the right balance is needed. Key decisions stay at the top, while routine ones are decentralised to outlets.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Violation of unity of command can weaken discipline and cause confusion.

**Reason (R):** When an employee receives conflicting orders from two superiors, he does not know whose order to follow.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: dual subordination leaves the employee confused about whom to obey, which undermines authority and discipline.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Fayol allowed a gang plank between employees at the same level in an emergency.

**Reason (R):** Fayol believed that the scalar chain should be removed altogether from organisations.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true. R is false: Fayol wanted the scalar chain to be followed normally; the gang plank is only a short-cut for emergencies, with superiors informed.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Unity of direction helps coordinate the activities of a division working towards one objective.

**Reason (R):** Unity of command prevents an employee from receiving orders from more than one boss.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both statements are true, but R does not explain A. R describes a different principle that concerns the individual employee, while A is about one head and one plan for a group of activities.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The principle of equity means that every employee must be paid exactly the same salary.
questions.solution_md: **False.** Equity means fairness and no discrimination; it does not mean identical pay. Pay should reflect the job and performance.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Under Fayol's gang plank, the superiors of the two employees must be kept informed of their direct communication.
questions.solution_md: **True.** The gang plank is a short-cut for speed, but the scalar chain is respected by keeping the superiors informed.

questions.stem_md: Team spirit and harmony among employees is called esprit de ___.
questions.solution_md: Esprit de corps means team spirit.

questions.stem_md: Match each imagined situation at a Nagpur logistics company with the Fayol principle it shows.

options.text_md: Drivers, loaders and dispatch clerks each do only their own task
Every forklift is parked in its marked bay after use
Each loader reports only to the shift supervisor
A loader who suggested a faster loading plan was rewarded

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Specialised tasks show division of work; a place for everything shows order; one boss per employee shows unity of command; rewarding suggestions shows initiative.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined company, the scalar chain runs from the managing director down to a machine operator. Arrange the positions from the highest to the lowest.
questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (b) → (d) → (c) → (a). The formal line of authority runs from the managing director through the works manager and the shift supervisor to the operator.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between unity of command and unity of direction on any three bases.
questions.solution_md: Three bases, each stating both sides.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Meaning:** unity of command means **one boss** for each employee; unity of direction means **one head and one plan** for a group of activities with the same objective.
2. **Aim:** the first prevents **dual subordination**; the second prevents **overlapping** of activities and secures coordination.
3. **Effect:** the first concerns the working of the **individual employee**; the second the working of the **organisation or division** as a whole.

questions.stem_md: What does Fayol mean by discipline, and what three things did he say it requires?
questions.solution_md: Meaning plus the three requirements.

answer.model_answer_md: **Discipline** is obedience to the **rules and employment agreements** of the organisation. It needs **good superiors at all levels**, **clear and fair agreements**, and **judicious use of penalties**.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined bank, a cashier (level E) must urgently contact a loans clerk (level K) at the same level in another department. Explain how Fayol's scalar chain and gang plank apply.
questions.solution_md: Describe the normal route, then the emergency short-cut with superiors informed.

answer.model_answer_md: Normally the message would go **up the scalar chain** from E to the common superior and **down** to K, which takes time. In an urgent case, Fayol allows a **gang plank**: E contacts K **directly**, and both keep their **superiors informed**.

marking_scheme.step: Normal route along the scalar chain

questions.stem_md: State the principle of esprit de corps and give one way in which the manager of a school canteen could apply it.
questions.solution_md: The principle plus a realistic way to apply it.

answer.model_answer_md: **Esprit de corps** means promoting **team spirit, unity and harmony** among employees. The canteen manager could praise the whole team for a successful sports day lunch, saying **we**, not **I**, and share credit with every worker.

questions.stem_md: An imagined BPO in Noida pays far below other firms in the area and replaces staff every few months. Name the two principles of Fayol being violated and explain one effect on the business.
questions.solution_md: Two principles named and linked to the facts, then one effect.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Remuneration of employees** is violated: pay is not fair or enough for a reasonable standard of living.
2. **Stability of tenure of personnel** is violated: staff are replaced before they learn the job.
3. **Effect:** high **employee turnover** raises costs of hiring and training, and inexperienced staff give **poor service**, so customers may leave.

marking_scheme.step: Stability of tenure violated with reason

questions.stem_md: Explain any five of Fayol's principles of management, with one example from an imagined hospital for each.
questions.solution_md: Five principles, each explained with a hospital example.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Division of work:** surgeons, nurses and lab technicians each do specialised work, raising efficiency.
2. **Unity of command:** each nurse takes orders from **one** ward sister only.
3. **Order:** medicines are stored in labelled places so they are found at once.
4. **Equity:** patients' families and staff are treated fairly, without discrimination.
5. **Esprit de corps:** the casualty team shares credit for saving lives, building team spirit.

questions.stem_md: At an imagined pickle-making unit in Guntur, workers receive orders from three supervisors, jars are kept wherever there is space, the owner promotes only relatives, and suggestions from workers are ignored. Identify the principles of Fayol being violated and suggest how the owner can correct each.
questions.solution_md: Four principles identified from the lines of the case, each with a correction, and a concluding point.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Unity of command:** three supervisors give orders; each worker should report to **one** supervisor.
2. **Order:** jars lie anywhere; fix a **marked place** for raw materials and finished jars.
3. **Equity:** promoting only relatives is unfair; promote on **merit**.
4. **Initiative:** ignoring suggestions kills interest; start a **suggestion scheme** with rewards.
5. **Overall:** applying these principles reduces confusion and waste and improves morale.

marking_scheme.step: Unity of command identified and corrected

questions.stem_md: Taylor's principle **science, not rule of thumb** means

options.text_md: managers should rely on their past habits and guesses
workers should decide their own methods without guidance
only scientists should be hired as managers
every task should be studied scientifically to find the one best method

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** every task should be studied scientifically to find the one best method. Taylor wanted decisions based on study and experiment rather than on habit or guesswork (rule of thumb).

questions.stem_md: Which change did Taylor call a **mental revolution**?

options.text_md: Management and workers changing their attitude from conflict to cooperation, sharing the gains
Moving the factory to a new city
Paying all workers the same wage

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Management and workers changing their attitude from conflict to cooperation, sharing the gains. Mental revolution means both sides see that they gain together; harmony replaces discord.

questions.stem_md: A consultant at an imagined shoe factory in Agra films workers stitching soles and removes three needless hand movements from each cycle. This is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** motion study. Studying the movements in a job to remove unnecessary ones is motion study. Time study fixes the standard time; fatigue study fixes rest intervals.

questions.stem_md: At an imagined mobile-phone assembly unit in Noida, an engineer times many trained workers fitting a screen and fixes 4 minutes as the standard. Which technique is this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Time study. Fixing the standard time for a well-defined job by observing it is time study, which also helps decide wages and the number of workers.

questions.stem_md: After studying output through the day, an imagined brick kiln in Bihar fixes a 10-minute break every 90 minutes for its moulders. Which technique did it use?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Fatigue study. Fatigue study finds the amount and frequency of rest needed so that workers regain energy and output does not fall.

questions.stem_md: An imagined dairy in Anand compares three ways of packing milk pouches, from receiving the milk to loading the crates, and chooses the one with the least cost and time. This is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** method study. Method study looks at the whole sequence of an operation to find the one best way of doing it.

questions.stem_md: An imagined paint company in Thane cuts its range of tin sizes from 14 to 5, removing sizes that hardly sell. This technique is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** simplification of work. Simplification eliminates unnecessary varieties, sizes and grades. Standardisation sets fixed standards for a process or product.

questions.stem_md: Under functional foremanship, Taylor proposed how many specialist foremen in all?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Eight. Eight: four under the planning in-charge and four under the production in-charge.

questions.stem_md: In functional foremanship, who ensures that machines are run at the right speed and work is completed on time?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Speed boss. The speed boss sees that tasks are done on time and at the proper speed. The gang boss keeps machines and tools ready; the route clerk fixes the route of work; the disciplinarian enforces rules.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following foremen works under the **planning in-charge**?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Instruction card clerk. Under the planning in-charge are the route clerk, instruction card clerk, time and cost clerk and disciplinarian. The repair boss, inspector, gang boss and speed boss work under the production in-charge.

questions.stem_md: The main purpose of Taylor's differential piece wage system is to

options.text_md: pay every worker the same fixed salary
reward efficient workers with a higher rate and motivate others to reach the standard
reduce the wages of all workers
pay workers according to their years of service

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** reward efficient workers with a higher rate and motivate others to reach the standard. Workers who reach the standard output get a higher rate per piece; those below it get a lower rate, which rewards efficiency.

questions.stem_md: Managers at an imagined pump factory in Coimbatore invite workers' suggestions and share the savings with them. Which principle of Taylor is this?

options.text_md: Development of each and every person

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Cooperation, not individualism. Taylor wanted management and workers to work together, with management welcoming workers' suggestions and both sharing the gains: cooperation, not individualism.

questions.stem_md: An imagined electronics firm in Bengaluru tests applicants for finger dexterity, places them on suitable jobs and trains them in the best method. Which principle of Taylor does this follow?

options.text_md: Development of each and every person to his or her greatest efficiency and prosperity

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Development of each and every person to his or her greatest efficiency and prosperity. Scientific selection, placement and training of each worker develop them to their greatest efficiency and prosperity.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Functional foremanship violates Fayol's principle of unity of command.

**Reason (R):** Under functional foremanship, a worker receives instructions from eight specialist foremen.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: with eight foremen giving instructions, a worker has more than one boss, which is against unity of command.

**Assertion (A):** Under the differential piece wage system, a worker who produces below the standard earns less per piece.

**Reason (R):** The system uses two piece rates: a higher rate for output at or above the standard and a lower rate below it.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: the lower rate applies to output below the standard.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Taylor developed his ideas mainly from his experience as a top manager, while Fayol developed his ideas from experiments on the shop floor.
questions.solution_md: **False.** It is the other way round: Taylor worked through observation and experiment on the shop floor, while Fayol drew on his experience as a top manager.

questions.stem_md: At an imagined hosiery unit in Ludhiana the standard output is 20 pieces a day. The rate is ₹12 a piece at or above the standard and ₹9 a piece below it. Arjun makes 24 pieces and Kabir makes 16 pieces in a day. By how many rupees do Arjun's daily earnings exceed Kabir's?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Arjun is above the standard, so he earns 24 × 12 = ₹288.
Step 2: Kabir is below the standard, so he earns 16 × 9 = ₹144.
Step 3: Difference = 288 − 144 = ₹144.

questions.stem_md: Using the same hosiery unit (standard 20 pieces; ₹12 at or above the standard, ₹9 below it), what does Kabir earn for 16 pieces in a day (in ₹)?
questions.solution_md: 16 is below the standard of 20, so the lower rate applies: 16 × 9 = ₹144.

questions.stem_md: Under functional foremanship, the ___ boss keeps machines and tools ready for work, and the ___ checks the quality of work.
questions.solution_md: The gang boss keeps machines, tools and materials ready, and the inspector checks quality.

questions.stem_md: Match each technique of scientific management with what it decides at an imagined bicycle factory in Ludhiana.

match_right.text_md: Cutting frame sizes from twelve to four
How often painters take a rest
Which hand movements in wheel truing can be dropped
Standard time to fit a chain

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(s), (b)–(q), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Time study sets standard times; fatigue study sets rest intervals; motion study removes needless movements; simplification removes unnecessary varieties.

questions.stem_md: Explain the principle of harmony, not discord, and the idea of mental revolution behind it.
questions.solution_md: State the principle and explain the change in attitude it requires.

answer.model_answer_md: Taylor said there should be **harmony** between management and workers, not class conflict. This needs a **mental revolution**: both change their attitude, management **shares gains** with workers and workers work with full effort, so both prosper.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between standardisation and simplification of work.
questions.solution_md: Define each and bring out the difference.

answer.model_answer_md: **Standardisation** sets fixed **standards** for every activity: the process, raw materials, tools, time and quality. **Simplification** removes **unnecessary diversity** of products, such as extra sizes, types and grades, to cut cost.

questions.stem_md: Explain functional foremanship and name the specialists under the planning in-charge and the production in-charge.
questions.solution_md: Explain the idea and list all eight under the right head.

answer.model_answer_md:
Taylor separated **planning from execution** and gave each worker **specialist** foremen, each an expert in one function.
The four who plan, under the planning in-charge, are the **route clerk**, the **instruction card clerk**, the **time and cost clerk** and the **disciplinarian**.
The four who supervise production are the **speed boss**, the **gang boss**, the **repair boss** and the **inspector**.

marking_scheme.step: Concept: separation of planning and execution with specialists

questions.stem_md: The owner of an imagined tailoring unit in Kanpur finds that orders are late, workers tire by afternoon and each tailor stitches a shirt differently. Suggest one technique of scientific management for each problem.
questions.solution_md: Each problem matched to a suitable technique, with a reason.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Late orders: time study**, to fix the standard time for each shirt and plan the number of tailors needed.
2. **Tired workers: fatigue study**, to fix rest breaks so energy and output are kept up.
3. **Different methods: method study** (with standardisation), to find and fix the **one best way** to stitch a shirt.

questions.stem_md: Compare the contributions of Fayol and Taylor on any three bases.
questions.solution_md: Three bases, each with both sides.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Perspective:** Fayol looked at management from the **top level**; Taylor from the **shop floor** (supervisory level).
2. **Unity of command:** Fayol held to it strictly; Taylor's **functional foremanship** gives a worker eight bosses.
3. **Basis:** Fayol relied on **personal experience** as a manager; Taylor on **observation and experiments**. (Also: focus on administration vs productivity; universal vs specific application.)

questions.stem_md: Explain Taylor's principles of scientific management.
questions.solution_md: All four principles explained, with the overall result.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Science, not rule of thumb:** every job is studied scientifically to find the **one best method**, replacing habit and guesswork.
2. **Harmony, not discord:** management and workers should end conflict through a **mental revolution**, seeing that they gain together.
3. **Cooperation, not individualism:** management should welcome **workers' suggestions** and share gains, and workers should not strike without cause.
4. **Development of each and every person:** **scientific selection**, placement and **training** to bring out each worker's greatest efficiency and prosperity.
5. **Result:** higher productivity, higher wages and lower costs for both sides.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between the contributions of Fayol and Taylor on any five bases.
questions.solution_md: Five bases, each with both sides.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Perspective:** Fayol: top management; Taylor: shop-floor supervision.
2. **Unity of command:** Fayol followed it strictly; Taylor broke it through **functional foremanship**.
3. **Applicability:** Fayol's principles are **universal**; Taylor's suit **specialised situations**.
4. **Basis:** Fayol: **personal experience**; Taylor: **observation and experimentation**.
5. **Focus:** Fayol: improving **overall administration**; Taylor: raising **productivity**. (Also: Fayol a practitioner, Taylor a scientist; general theory of administration vs scientific management.)

questions.stem_md: An imagined toy factory in Channapatna wants to raise output without hiring more workers. Explain five techniques of scientific management it could use.
questions.solution_md: Five techniques, each applied to the factory.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Method study:** find the **one best way** to cut, turn and lacquer each toy.
2. **Motion study:** remove **needless movements** of the turners' hands.
3. **Time study:** fix a **standard time** per toy to plan work and pay.
4. **Fatigue study:** schedule **rest breaks** so workers keep up their output.
5. **Differential piece wage:** pay a **higher rate** to those who reach the standard, motivating everyone to improve.

The new operations head, Ms Kaur, gave every parcel route a numbered bay and **told each sorter to take orders only from his shift leader**. She also started a monthly award for the best idea to speed up sorting; a sorter's idea of colour-coded tags cut errors by half.

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined business situation written by SOYL for practice.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Separate heads and plans for each unit is unity of direction.

**(b)** Fair pay within the firm's capacity is the principle of remuneration.

**(c) (i)** Name the principle and explain the cost of frequent moves.

**OR (c) (ii)** Name the principle and link it to the words used.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Unity of direction**: one head and one plan for each group of activities with the same objective.

**(b)** **Remuneration of employees**: pay should be fair and give a reasonable standard of living.

**(c) (i)** **Stability of tenure of personnel.** Moving new pluckers every few weeks meant they never learnt a garden well, so **efficiency fell** and the cost of training rose; settled workers become productive.

**OR (c) (ii)** **Esprit de corps.** By thanking "all of us" he uses **we**, not I, and gives credit to the whole team, which builds **team spirit and unity**.

questions.passage_md:
**Brahmaputra Leaf Tea Estate, Assam (imagined)**

The estate has two units: one grows and plucks tea, the other runs a packaging plant. Each unit has its own manager and its own targets. Last season the pluckers were paid less than in nearby estates, and many left mid-season; the new ones were moved between gardens every few weeks. The general manager, Mr Bora, has now raised wages to match the area and **promised that pluckers will stay in the same garden for the whole season**. At the season-end festival he thanked "all of us at Brahmaputra Leaf" for a record crop.

children.stem_md: Name the principle Mr Bora followed by raising wages to match the area.

answer.model_answer_md: **Remuneration of employees**: pay should be fair and give a reasonable standard of living.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Which principle does Mr Bora's festival speech reflect? Explain.

answer.model_answer_md: **Esprit de corps.** By thanking "all of us" he uses **we**, not I, and gives credit to the whole team, which builds **team spirit and unity**.

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined situation written by SOYL for practice.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** The same principles work in a hotel and a school canteen.

**(b)** The canteen's interest comes before the manager's personal interest.

**(c) (i)** Name the feature and explain with the case.

**OR (c) (ii)** Name the principle and one benefit.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Universal applicability**: principles apply to business and non-business organisations alike.

**(b)** The manager's personal interest gave way to the school's: this is **subordination of individual interest to general interest**.

**(c) (i)** **Flexible** (also contingent): principles are not rigid; the principal **modified** them to suit the small canteen, showing that their application depends on the **situation**.

**OR (c) (ii)** **Division of work.** Each person does a specialised task, so work is done **faster and with fewer mistakes**.

questions.passage_md:
**Navodaya Public School canteen, Shimla (imagined)**

The school's principal, who had once managed a hotel kitchen, used the same management principles to run the canteen. She split the work: two cooks, one cashier and one helper for cleaning. When the canteen manager wanted to buy vegetables at a higher price from a friend's shop, the principal asked him to buy from the cheapest good-quality supplier, since the canteen served the whole school. She **found that strict rules suited the large hotel but adapted them for the small canteen**, where staff now help each other at lunch hour.
